paras: The killing of Lewis C. Lane took place near Quitman, Georgia, on July 16, 1888, when W. T. Arrington overtook a sheriff who was moving Lane, a Savannah traveling salesman charged with assaulting Arrington's daughter, to the Thomasville jail and shot him dead. Arrington and his brother-in-law Henry T. Williams were later charged with murder and released on bail, and no report of a trial was found. The Savannah Morning News covered the case at length because Lane was well known there, and a letter in its columns called the killing lynch law.

Lane, about 26, had lived in Savannah for four years; his mother still lived in Quitman, his former home. He had been calling on Missouri Arrington, the daughter of a farmer living just outside the town. According to her statement to the coroner's jury, Lane drove her into a swamp on Sunday, July 15, and seized her by the throat when she tried to leave the buggy.

That evening her father and a companion came to Lane's mother's house with shotguns, and Arrington said he had come to kill Lane, who replied that he would marry the young woman and had only been testing her virtue. He was arrested that night on a charge of attempted felonious assault and released on bond, then re-arrested Monday morning on a charge of assault and jailed.

Fearing an attempt to lynch Lane, the sheriff decided to move him to Thomasville. Sheriff McNeill and a deputy left the jail with Lane between 4 and 5 o'clock and turned onto a trail to avoid pursuit. Arrington and two others took a horse at pistol point and rode after them.

About five miles from town, the three armed men stopped the deputy and forced him at gunpoint to lead them to the prisoner. Arrington leveled his shotgun at Lane, who turned to the sheriff for protection, and the sheriff, "overpowered," turned his back as Lane was shot. Wounded in the back, Lane fired a revolver over the sheriff's shoulder and missed; when he fell, Arrington put the gun to his left ear and fired again.

A Quitman visitor told the Morning News that public sentiment there was against Lane and that the coroner's jury had found the killing justifiable. By July 26 Lane's friends had obtained warrants for Arrington and Williams, said to have urged the shooting, and a Quitman citizen said local opinion opposed "individuals taking the law into their hands."

In early August another brother-in-law, M. H. Williams, received an anonymous letter signed "Many Friends of Lane" telling him to leave town. Lane's relatives denounced the letter in the Quitman Free Press, writing that they asked only that the killing be legally investigated. On August 6 Judge Hansell, at Thomasville, allowed bail of $5,000 each to Arrington and Williams without going into the merits, and they gave bond to appear at the next term of the Brooks County superior court. A Quitman report in December said the Arrington-Lane case would probably be tried at the term then opening, but no account of a trial or verdict appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News, Lane's home-city paper, carried the story on four straight days and followed the prosecution into December. Its headlines treated the assault as fact, describing "His Evil Deed" and "a Father's Fatal Revenge," while its stories stressed his popularity and his friends' surprise. The same paper printed a letter signed "Citizen" that described Lane as shot "without a hearing, without process of law" in the sheriff's custody and declared that "Lynch law must be stopped."

Beyond Savannah the case ran as a brief wire item, headed "A Father's Revenge" in the South Western News; a Virginia weekly's summary said the father shot the man who "had outrageously assaulted" his daughter, and the Marietta Journal noted the sheriff had moved Lane "to prevent lynching." None of the reports mentioned race.

The early dispatches named only the father as the attacker, while the detailed Quitman account had three armed men in the pursuit, and the later warrant charged Williams as well. The reported coroner's verdict of justifiable killing came second-hand and was followed within ten days by murder warrants.

reader.title: Killing of Lewis C. Lane
bases: A prisoner in the sheriff's charge was overtaken on the road by armed men led by his accuser's father, who forced the officers to give him up and shot him dead (A1, A3, A9).

Lane was killed without lawful authority while in custody by a party the detailed account puts at three armed men, acting in revenge for an alleged assault on the shooter's daughter (A3, A9, A11). The early reports name only the father, and one man fired, so the killing sits between a private revenge killing and a lynching; a Savannah letter called it 'lynch law' (A1, A4).

A Quitman dispatch, a Waycross special, a Savannah wire dispatch and a Quitman informant's detailed account agree that Lane was shot by the young woman's father while the sheriff was moving him from Quitman (A1, A3, A7).

accounts.label: Quitman dispatch and Waycross special
accounts.gist: Lane, arrested on a charge of assault with intent to rape, was being taken to Thomasville to save him from lynching when the young woman's father overtook the party; 'A fight ensued' and Lane was shot.

accounts.label: Quitman informant (R. E. L. McFarlin)
accounts.gist: Three armed men forced the deputy to lead them to the sheriff and prisoner; Arrington shot Lane in the back, Lane fired back and missed, and Arrington then shot him in the head.

accounts.label: Wire briefs
accounts.gist: A traveling salesman was shot at or near Quitman by the father of a girl he had assaulted or attempted to rape, while the sheriff was moving him to another town.

accounts.label: Lane's relatives
accounts.gist: In a card to the Quitman Free Press they denounced the threat to M. H. Williams and asked only that the killing be legally investigated.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News treated Lane's guilt as established in headlines ('His Evil Deed', 'A Father's Fatal Revenge') while stressing his popularity and printing the protest letter and the prosecution news.
A letter signed 'Citizen' called the killing lynch law and demanded that those who take the law into their own hands be dealt with.
Out-of-town papers ran one-sentence wire items under 'A Father's Revenge' or in news summaries, stating the assault as fact.

Three armed men; Williams with Arrington and urging him

conflicts.note: The later, more detailed Quitman sources name companions; the first reports were brief and lacked particulars.

versions.value: 'A fight ensued' and Lane was shot
Lane was shot in the back while sheltering behind the sheriff, fired once and missed, then was shot in the head

Warrants and a bail order on a charge of murder

conflicts.note: The coroner's verdict is reported second-hand by a Quitman visitor; the murder charge followed after Lane's friends pressed the prosecution.
Spelling variants; the Morning News's own reports use Lewis C. Lane and Arrington.

On the road from Quitman toward Thomasville, about five miles out of Quitman, on a trail off the public road

Charged first with attempted felonious assault, then with assault with intent to rape, on Missouri Arrington during a Sunday buggy drive; a wire brief stated the assault as fact
